tele-001.question: In the TRUST trial (Varma, Circulation 2010), automatic daily remote monitoring of ICDs (Biotronik Home Monitoring) mainly showed:
options: Fewer visits and event detection within 1–2 days, with safety maintained
A significant reduction in all-cause mortality at one year through early detection
A reduction in appropriate shocks thanks to prompt reprogramming
Longer lead longevity thanks to less frequent threshold measurements
commentaires: Correct: about 45% fewer in-hospital evaluations, events identified within 1–2 days versus more than a month, with no excess morbidity.
Incorrect: TRUST was not designed to show a mortality benefit.
Incorrect: appropriate shocks depend on the arrhythmia; remote monitoring does not reduce them per se.
Incorrect: remote monitoring detects lead malfunction earlier but does not extend lead lifespan.
tele-001.explication: TRUST randomised 1339 ICD recipients to automatic daily remote monitoring or conventional in-office follow-up. Remote monitoring reduced in-hospital evaluations by about 45% without increasing morbidity (safety endpoint), and events (AF, VT/VF, lead or generator problems) were identified after a median of 1–2 days versus more than a month with conventional follow-up. The trial was not designed to show a mortality benefit. Remote monitoring does not by itself change the number of appropriate shocks (which depends on the arrhythmia) or lead longevity, but it allows earlier detection of lead malfunction.
tele-001.aRetenir: TRUST: fewer visits, events detected within 1–2 days instead of more than a month, safety maintained.

tele-002.question: The French ECOST trial (Guédon-Moreau, Eur Heart J 2013) on remote monitoring of ICDs notably showed:
options: More appropriate shocks delivered, thanks to better VT detection
Non-inferior safety and roughly half as many inappropriate shocks
Superiority for cardiovascular mortality at two years of follow-up
A reduction in hospitalisations for acute decompensated heart failure
commentaires: Incorrect: remote monitoring does not change the occurrence of treated arrhythmias; its main effect is to reduce avoidable therapies.
Correct: non-inferior safety, about 52% fewer patients receiving inappropriate shocks and far fewer capacitor charges.
Incorrect: ECOST was not designed for mortality.
Incorrect: HF hospitalisations were not an ECOST endpoint.
tele-002.explication: ECOST randomised 433 ICD recipients in France to daily remote monitoring (Home Monitoring) or in-office follow-up. The primary safety endpoint (major adverse events) was non-inferior. Remote monitoring reduced the number of patients receiving inappropriate shocks by about 52% and markedly reduced capacitor charges, with a favourable effect on battery longevity. The reason is simple: lead noise, rapid AF or oversensing are picked up before they trigger therapy. ECOST was not designed to assess mortality or HF hospitalisations.
tele-002.aRetenir: ECOST: remote monitoring is safe and reduces inappropriate shocks and capacitor charges.

tele-003.question: Regarding the IN-TIME trial (Hindricks, Lancet 2014), which statement is correct?
options: It relied on scheduled quarterly transmissions, with no alerts
It showed more hospitalisations, driven by false alerts
It improved a composite clinical score, with lower mortality
It enrolled single-chamber pacemaker patients without heart failure
commentaires: Incorrect: IN-TIME relied on automatic daily multiparameter transmission.
Incorrect: no excess of alert-related hospitalisations was reported.
Correct: fewer patients with a worsened Packer score (18.9% vs 27.2%) and lower all-cause mortality in the remote monitoring arm.
Incorrect: patients had heart failure (NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤35%) and a dual-chamber ICD or CRT-D.
tele-003.explication: IN-TIME enrolled 664 heart failure patients (NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤35%) with a dual-chamber ICD or CRT-D, using automatic daily multiparameter remote monitoring (atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, % BiV pacing, PVCs, activity, etc.). The proportion of patients whose composite score worsened was lower in the remote monitoring arm (18.9% vs 27.2%), and all-cause mortality was also lower. The key is the combination of automatic daily transmission with an organised response (structured telephone contact). Scheduled quarterly transmissions are not the IN-TIME model. The pitfall: this benefit has not been reproduced in every trial, hence the importance of the organisation that responds to alerts.
tele-003.aRetenir: IN-TIME: daily multiparameter remote monitoring + structured response = less clinical worsening in device patients with HF.

tele-004.question: The EVOLVO trial (Landolina, Circulation 2012), which used CareLink with OptiVol alerts in HF patients with an ICD/CRT-D, showed:
options: Fewer urgent contacts (emergency or unscheduled visits) for HF or arrhythmia
More unscheduled visits, triggered by false OptiVol alerts
A halving of all-cause mortality at 16 months of follow-up
No effect on urgent contacts, the device audible alarm being just as effective
commentaires: Correct: this was the primary endpoint, reduced by about 35%, with a shorter time to clinical decision.
Incorrect: urgent or unscheduled visits actually fell by about 35%.
Incorrect: with 200 patients, EVOLVO was not powered for mortality.
Incorrect: remotely transmitted alerts proved more effective than the audible alarm, which patients often fail to hear.
tele-004.explication: EVOLVO randomised 200 HF device patients to remote monitoring with alerts (including the OptiVol fluid index) or standard follow-up with office visits and the device audible alarm. The primary endpoint, the number of emergency department or unscheduled visits for HF, arrhythmia or ICD-related events, was reduced by about 35%. The time from event to clinical decision was also shortened. The trial was not powered for mortality. It shows that an automatically transmitted alert is more effective than the audible alarm, which patients often fail to hear.
tele-004.aRetenir: EVOLVO: remote alerts reduce urgent healthcare use and shorten the time to clinical decision.

tele-005.question: True or false: in a pacemaker or ICD patient on remote monitoring, in-person follow-up can be dropped altogether and no further clinic visits are needed.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: in-person visits are spaced out, not abolished (wound check, examination, education, planning of generator replacement).
Correct: remote monitoring is combined with at least one in-person evaluation, classically once a year; only the implantable loop recorder can do without it.
tele-005.explication: The 2015 HRS consensus recommends combining remote monitoring with at least one annual in-person evaluation, rather than calendar-based in-person follow-up alone. The 2023 consensus on the practical management of the remote monitoring clinic goes further: with a continuous and reliable connection, alert-driven follow-up allows scheduled visits to be spaced out even more, but it does not abolish them. The post-implant wound check, clinical examination, some measurements, patient education and planning of generator replacement remain in person, and any loss of connectivity, recent alert or comorbidity calls for more frequent visits. Some situations also require an in-person check (reprogramming, suspected malfunction). The pitfall is to believe that remote monitoring "replaces" the cardiologist; only the implantable loop recorder, a purely diagnostic device, may no longer need routine clinic visits after the wound check.
tele-005.aRetenir: Remote monitoring spaces out in-person visits (classically at least one a year) but does not abolish them.

tele-006.question: The French COMPAS trial (Mabo, Eur Heart J 2012) studied:
options: Pacemaker patients: non-inferiority, with far fewer clinic visits
Loop recorder patients with syncope: faster diagnosis
Smartwatch-detected AF: fewer strokes on a direct oral anticoagulant
CRT-D patients with severe HF: fewer HF hospitalisations
commentaires: Correct: 538 pacemaker patients, non-inferior safety and about 56% fewer outpatient visits.
Incorrect: COMPAS did not study implantable loop recorders.
Incorrect: COMPAS dealt neither with smartwatches nor with anticoagulation.
Incorrect: this is closer to the IN-TIME population; COMPAS involved pacemaker patients.
tele-006.explication: COMPAS randomised 538 pacemaker patients to remote monitoring (Home Monitoring) or in-office follow-up. The safety endpoint (major adverse events) was non-inferior and outpatient visits were reduced by about 56%. Hospitalisations for atrial arrhythmia (6 vs 18) and for stroke (2 vs 8) were less frequent in the remote monitoring arm, thanks to earlier detection of arrhythmias. It is one of the main pieces of evidence supporting remote monitoring of pacemakers, and not only of ICDs.
tele-006.aRetenir: COMPAS: remote monitoring is safe in pacemaker patients and substantially reduces clinic visits.

tele-007.question: Which of the following benefits have been demonstrated by randomised trials of remote monitoring of cardiac implantable electronic devices?
options: Earlier detection of arrhythmic and technical events
Fewer inappropriate shocks in ICD patients
Fewer in-person visits with no loss of safety
Complete elimination of the risk of sudden cardiac death
Reduced all-cause mortality found in every trial
commentaires: Correct: TRUST showed detection within 1–2 days instead of more than a month.
Correct: ECOST roughly halved inappropriate shocks.
Correct: TRUST and COMPAS reduced visits with no loss of safety.
Incorrect: it is the ICD that treats the arrhythmia; remote monitoring only monitors and anticipates.
Incorrect: the mortality benefit remains debated; IN-TIME was positive, other trials neutral.
tele-007.explication: TRUST showed event detection within 1–2 days instead of more than a month, and fewer visits. COMPAS confirmed fewer visits in pacemaker patients. ECOST showed fewer inappropriate shocks and fewer capacitor charges, which preserves the battery. On the other hand, remote monitoring obviously does not "eliminate" the risk of sudden cardiac death: the ICD treats the arrhythmia, while remote monitoring only serves to monitor and anticipate. The mortality benefit remains debated and depends on the organisation that responds to alerts (IN-TIME positive, other trials neutral). The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines acknowledge that device-based monitoring detects malfunction and arrhythmias, but consider its clinical benefit for HF management (impedance, multiparameter algorithms) poorly demonstrated and make no recommendation, unlike pulmonary artery pressure monitoring (class IIa).
tele-007.aRetenir: Established benefits: early detection, fewer visits, fewer inappropriate shocks, preserved battery.

tele-008.question: True or false: patients on remote monitoring must be told that remote monitoring is not an emergency service and that, if they have serious symptoms, they must call the emergency services (15 in France).
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: transmissions are reviewed during working hours; with serious symptoms, the patient calls the emergency services (15).
Incorrect: no clinic reviews transmissions 24/7; suggesting otherwise leaves the patient waiting for a call-back that will not come in time.
tele-008.explication: Transmissions are reviewed during working hours: the 2023 HRS consensus asks for alerts to be handled within the working day, prioritising critical alerts, but no clinic provides 24/7 review. The 2023 HRS consensus emphasises patient education at enrolment: what remote monitoring does, what it does not do, and what to do in case of symptoms (presyncope, syncope, repeated shocks, chest pain). In France, life-threatening emergencies are handled by the SAMU (15). The classic pitfall: a patient who receives several shocks and "waits for the clinic to call".
tele-008.aRetenir: Remote monitoring is not real-time surveillance: emergency = call the emergency services (15).

tele-009.question: According to the 2023 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS consensus, when should a patient ideally be enrolled in remote monitoring after implantation of a cardiac device?
options: At the first in-person check, 3 months after implantation
As early as possible, ideally before hospital discharge
Only if an arrhythmia is detected at the first check
After one year, once lead stability has been established
commentaires: Incorrect: the first weeks are the high-risk period (lead dislodgement, threshold rise); waiting 3 months forfeits this monitoring.
Correct: enrolment and pairing before discharge, at the latest within 2 weeks (2023 HRS consensus).
Incorrect: remote monitoring is not conditional on an event; its very purpose is to detect one.
Incorrect: a patient not connected at the outset is often connected much later, or never.
tele-009.explication: The consensus recommends enrolling the patient and pairing the transmitter as early as possible, ideally before discharge and at the latest within 2 weeks of implantation; for an implantable loop recorder, enrolment before discharge is mandatory. The first weeks are precisely the period at risk of lead dislodgement, threshold rise or complications, and a patient not connected at the outset is often connected much later, or never. Waiting for the first check or for an event defeats the purpose of early monitoring. Early enrolment also makes it possible to confirm that the connection works from the start.
tele-009.aRetenir: Enrol and pair for remote monitoring before hospital discharge.

tele-010.question: In a remote monitoring clinic, what is the expected role of the remote monitoring nurse working under a written protocol?
options: Triage alerts according to the protocol and escalate to the physician
Remotely reprogram the ICD therapy zones according to the protocol
Independently start an anticoagulant for AF confirmed on the EGM
Close alerts judged benign without any physician review
commentaires: Correct: first-line triage, patient contact, documentation and escalation to the physician according to the written protocol.
Incorrect: reprogramming is the physician's responsibility, and remote programming of zones is not a routine function.
Incorrect: the treatment decision (anticoagulation) rests with the physician.
Incorrect: the protocol defines the sign-off pathways; the nurse does not close alerts alone outside this framework.
tele-010.explication: The remote monitoring nurse (or technician/physiologist) provides first-line review: reading transmissions, triaging alerts according to defined criteria and urgency levels, contacting the patient, checking connectivity and documentation. Situations specified in the protocol are passed to the physician, who retains the treatment decision (anticoagulation, antiarrhythmic drugs, reprogramming). In France, delegated acts are only possible within a formal cooperation protocol. Moreover, remote programming of ICD zones is not a routine feature of current remote monitoring systems.
tele-010.aRetenir: Nurse = first-line triage and escalation according to protocol; treatment decision = physician.

tele-011.question: Which elements should be included in a remote monitoring clinic's written alert management protocol?
options: Urgency levels, each with an associated response time
Review of every transmission by the physician before the nurse
Documentation of actions in the patient record
What to do when transmissions stop arriving
Discontinuation of the annual in-person visit
commentaires: Correct: each alert type must have a priority level and a response time.
Incorrect: first-line triage is precisely delegated to the trained nurse or technician, with escalation to the physician.
Correct: every action must be documented, which also has medico-legal implications.
Correct: a disconnected patient is no longer monitored; the protocol must state who calls and within what time frame.
Incorrect: this has no place in an alert protocol and runs counter to the guidelines.
tele-011.explication: The 2023 HRS consensus recommends written protocols defining who does what, within what time frame and how it is documented: urgency level of each alert type, response times, escalation pathway (nurse to physician, physician to patient or emergency services), how the patient is contacted, and documentation. First-line triage is performed by trained non-physician staff: having the physician review every transmission first would invert the workflow and overwhelm the team. Loss of connectivity must also be managed, because a disconnected patient is no longer monitored. Discontinuing the annual visit is not part of an alert protocol and runs counter to the guidelines.
tele-011.aRetenir: An alert protocol = urgency levels + response times + escalation + documentation + management of lost connectivity.

tele-012.question: Describe briefly the typical organisation of a remote monitoring clinic for cardiac implantable electronic devices, from transmitted signal to clinical decision.
tele-012.reponseAttendue: Enrolment and pairing before discharge, with patient education (it is not an emergency service). Receipt of transmissions and alerts on the manufacturer's platform. First-line triage by a trained nurse or technician according to a written protocol (urgency levels, response times). Escalation to the physician (electrophysiologist) for the alerts specified. Patient contact and decision (no action, clinic visit, treatment adjustment, reprogramming, emergency department). Documentation in the patient record. Management of lost connectivity. In-person visits maintained, spaced out according to the protocol (classically at least once a year).
tele-012.explication: The 2023 HRS consensus describes a team-based model with defined roles: trained non-physician staff for first-line review, physicians responsible for decisions, and written protocols so that every alert has a priority level and a response time. The patient's connectivity must be actively monitored, because an unplugged transmitter makes monitoring illusory. Every action must be documented, which also has medico-legal implications. Patient education underpins safety: patients must know when to call the emergency services (15 in France). The pitfall is to organise the receipt of alerts without organising the response.
tele-012.aRetenir: Effective remote monitoring = early connection + protocol-based triage + physician escalation + documentation.
